newsitem.title: UK: Long nights journey into day for London Traders. [CORRECTED 09:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Long nights journey into day for London Traders. [CORRECTED 09:30 GMT]

text.p: Many of London's investment banks and stockbrokers decided that the British election was over months ago and did not keep an all-night vigil in the early hours of Friday -- the day the Labour Party returned from 18 years in opposition with a landslide victory over the ruling Conservatives.

But some die-hard dealers did stay at their desks, most of whom were too young to remember the last Labour government and the 1978-79 "winter of discontent" -- an event that helped sweep Margaret Thatcher into power.

"I was only 10. I've only known the Tories," Mark Shepherd, currency trader at Bank of America (BoA) said, as he stared at his flickering terminals just after midnight. "But, I'm not too worried. Labour's policies seem to be much the same as the Tories."

In the winter months before the May 1979 election strikes caused London morgues to overflow with corpses and provided a feast for rats who gorged on mounds of uncollected rubbish in Leicester Square, in the heart of the capital's theatre district.

The antics of powerful trades unions convinced a strike-weary public to embrace free-market principles of Thatcherism. It also forced Labour to break its ties with the unions, woo the business community and financial markets, and consign its interventionist policies to the dustbin.
"At the end of the day, what (Federal Reserve chairman) Alan Greenspan does is now of more importance than the politics," Shepherd said.

Richard Hill, head of foreign exchange trading at the BoA, is the only one of his currency cohorts with silver streaks in his hair and the sole dealer in the cavernous trading room who does remember the last Labour government.

Slumped in his chair, coffee in hand, dying for a cigarette in the non-smoking office, gawping at a large TV screen that was flashing "Labour Landslide", Hill is in despair -- but not because of the change of government.

"This is pathetic. We've only had five phone calls. Nobody is doing any business." To break the monotony, he leapt from his chair when a phone call lit up a multi-line switchboard. "Hey, that's number six. Now we're moving."

The sarcastic comment caused a brief chuckle from members of the graveyard shift, but the dealing room which would normally be buzzing with tens of millions of dollars of currency trades every minute, soon fell silent.
There was little business tonight.

Like his junior colleague, Hill was only expecting a reaction in value of the pound if the British electorate had defied the polls and voted for a hung parliament --where no party had overall control.
"That would have created uncertainty which no markets like. But there's no mystery tonight, people just wanted a change."
Hill did manage to "shift" a bit of sterling later on "but it was nothing too exciting."

At the last election vigil in 1992, trading rooms geared up for a hectic night amid polls that showed Labour and the Conservatives neck and neck. The Conservatives pulled off a surprise victory which sent the pound and gilts soaring.
The only thing BOA staff and share traders at stockbrokers Instinet were gearing up for was new ideas on how to stay awake as more and more previous safe Conservative seats fell to Labour.

"The uncertainity of the last few months being over, tired dealers look forward to a long Bank Holiday weekend before a fresh start next week," said Christian Frenzel, head of UK share dealing at Instinet, the agency broker wholly owned by Reuters Holdings Plc.
The head of share trading at a major investment bank said it was a waste of time keeping the candles burning this time but it had to be done, just in case something extraordinary had happened.
"Institutions aren't going to make the same mistake they did five years ago when they bought stock at crazy prices in the middle of the night," the trader, who wished to remain anonymous said.
"They woke up the next morning and found they could buy the same stock at five to ten percent less. It was a good lesson." (Corrects by clarifying trader's statement)
A sliver of light struck the Bank of America building as dawn made a tentative move down the narrow streets in London's "Square Mile" financial district.

It's not a Tory blue sky, but it is clear blue with just a hint of red on the horizon. Labour has won, the markets haven't melted, the sun has risen and weary, bored and blurry eyed dealers expect it to come out again tomorrow.
